intro: Tuatapere is a small town in western Southland, near the south coast of New Zealand's South Island and the edge of Fiordland. Inland from it, off Lillburn Monowai Road, a nature walk leads into dense, wet forest of moss and ferns. On that walk stands a great Hall's totara, a single column of peeling grey and red-brown bark that the sign at its foot measures at 8.31 metres round and puts at about a thousand years old.

trees.story:
The sign beside this trunk gives it a girth of 8.31 metres at chest height and an age of about a thousand years. It stands on the totara trees nature walk off Lillburn Monowai Road, in the Southland hills inland from Tuatapere, and a reader sent it to us with a GPS fix taken at its foot and a photograph of that sign.

The sign names it Halls Totara, Podocarpus hallii, the species botanists now list as Podocarpus laetus. It does not say how the age was reached, so take the thousand years as the estimate the sign calls it.

The reader's photograph looks up the trunk from its root plate. A single column rises out of the moss, far wider than a person could reach round, its bark grey and red-brown and peeling in long vertical strips, with cushions of moss climbing it. The trunk runs straight out of the top of the frame. Around it the forest is dense, wet and green, with ferns, mossy branches and smaller trees pressing in.

Eight metres round is a trunk that takes five or six people with arms outstretched to circle. Follow the walk into the forest and look for the widest trunk on it, with the green and yellow sign at its foot.
